summary: Lists requirements for robust IP/UDP/RTP header compression, drawn from the ROHC charter, working group discussions and 3GPP and 3G.IP input. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before building a tool, you write down what it must do. This is that list for shrinking packet labels on shaky links.

questions: why was crtp not good enough
what is error propagation in header compression
subtitle: The checklist that robust header compression for voice and video over cellular links had to meet.

tldr.problem: Real-time voice and video over cellular links carry IP, UDP and RTP headers that waste scarce radio capacity, and the existing scheme (CRTP, RFC 2508) suffers badly from error propagation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for a new scheme from the ROHC working group, grouped into impact on the Internet, supported headers, and efficiency on lossy, high-delay links.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. A protocol meeting it, such as ROHC in RFC 3095, is named as an example.

today: RFC 3096 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The protocol it names as an example of one meeting these requirements is in RFC 3095.

sections.title: Goal and Context
sections.content:
The ROHC (Robust Header Compression) working group aims to develop header compression schemes that perform well over links with high error rates and long link round trip times. Cellular links built with technologies such as WCDMA, EDGE and CDMA-2000 are the main target, but the schemes should suit other future high-loss, long-delay links.

The requirements are "more or less arbitrarily" divided into three groups: impact on Internet infrastructure, which headers must be compressed, and efficiency. They are driven by voice over IP and other real-time services in standards such as GERAN and UTRAN, which need a suitable scheme before the Release 2000 standards are completed.
sections.eli5: Phone networks send tiny voice packets, and the labels on them take up a lot of room. The goal is a way to shrink those labels even when the radio link loses data.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Header Requirements
sections.content:
Two requirements protect the rest of the Internet. Transparency: a header that is compressed and then decompressed must be semantically identical to the original, or the packet must be discarded. Ubiquity: no modifications to existing IP (v4 or v6), UDP or RTP implementations.

For supported headers, the scheme must support both IPv4 and IPv6 and compress headers of arbitrary RTP streams (genericity). It should efficiently compress Mobile IP headers, including tunneled packets for IPv4 and the Routing Header, Binding Update Destination Option and Home Address option for IPv6. It should also handle headers containing IPSEC subheaders, though the encrypted part of an ESP header and the cryptographic data in an AH header cannot be compressed.
sections.eli5: The shrunk label must expand back to exactly the original, or the packet gets thrown away. And nobody should have to change their existing software to use it.

sections.title: Efficiency Requirements
sections.content:
The scheme must give low relative overhead and be better than RFC 2508 (CRTP) under equal conditions. Error propagation must be kept to an absolute minimum, meaning later headers should not be lost or damaged just because an earlier one was. The RFC says CRTP suffers severely from it.

  • Handover loss: loss events of length 150 milliseconds must be handled efficiently without propagating loss or damage.
  • Context recreation: when the compressor or decompressor moves to another node, ROHC must not introduce erroneous headers and should not introduce packet loss.
  • Misordering: packets reaching the compressor may be misordered, and moderate misordering (2-3 packets) should be handled efficiently.
  • Delay: the scheme must not noticeably add to end-to-end delay, for example by requiring a later header before an earlier one can be decompressed.
  • Residual errors: for a residual bit-error rate of at most 1e-5, the scheme must not increase the error rate.

Other requirements: it must work under all expected link delays, perform well across two or more cellular links, operate (possibly less efficiently) on unidirectional or multicast links without feedback, and allow restricting the number of frame sizes used.
sections.eli5: If one letter gets lost, the following letters should still be readable. The fix also must not make the mail slower or add more mistakes than it removes.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
A protocol built to these requirements, such as ROHC, must be able to compress packets containing IPSEC headers. The RFC states that the document by itself adds no security risks, though other security aspects may need consideration in such protocols.

Likewise, a protocol meeting these requirements will need the IANA to assign numbers, but this document by itself requires no IANA involvement.
sections.eli5: The list itself is safe, but whatever gets built from it must still work with encrypted packets.
